title: Engraved Ostrich Eggshells Reveal Early Humans' Geometric Mindset
summary:
What looks like a simple scratch may actually be a window into the ancient human mind. Researchers at the University of Bologna have conducted a systematic quantitative analysis of 112 engraved ostrich eggshell fragments from three sites in South Africa and Namibia. Their findings, published in PLOS One, reveal that these 60,000-year-old markings are far from random. Instead, they follow recurring geometric principles: parallel lines, right angles, and repeated patterns like grids and diamonds.

"These engravings are organized and consistent, and show mastery of geometric relationships," explained Professor Silvia Ferrara, who coordinated the study. "There is not only a process of repeating signs: there is real visuo-spatial planning, as if the authors already had an overall image of the figure in mind before engraving it." The team used geometric and statistical techniques never before applied to these artifacts, reconstructing the direction, angles, and paths of each line.

The eggshells were likely used as water containers, making the engravings part of functional objects. The capacity to arrange shapes according to consistent rules is considered a crucial sign of emerging abstract thought—a major milestone in human cognitive evolution. "Our analysis shows that Homo sapiens 60,000 years ago already possessed a remarkable ability to organize visual space according to abstract principles," said first author Valentina Decembrini. This discovery pushes back the timeline for complex symbolic behavior and suggests that the roots of writing and mathematics may lie in such early geometric expressions.
why_it_matters: Understanding how early humans thought helps us trace the origins of skills we still use—planning, mathematics, art—showing that these abilities are part of a long human journey, not just modern inventions.

background_read: Ostrich eggshells have been used as water containers for tens of thousands of years across Africa, and engraved fragments turn up at many archaeological sites.
The newly analyzed fragments, unearthed at three sites in South Africa and Namibia, date from the Middle Stone Age, a period when modern humans were refining their cognitive and symbolic abilities.
This study, led by researchers at the University of Bologna (a historic university in Italy founded in 1088), is the first to apply systematic geometric and statistical tools to these engravings.

The results join earlier finds—such as the abstract ochre engravings from Blombos Cave (a famous archaeological site in South Africa, about 73,000 years old)—to show that Homo sapiens engaged in deliberate visual expression long before European cave paintings.
Such discoveries are reshaping our understanding of when and how the human mind developed the capacity for mathematics and writing.

perspectives.description: Archaeologists and anthropologists gain stronger evidence that symbolic thinking emerged earlier than once assumed, enriching our picture of human cognitive evolution and helping identify the behavioural foundations of later cultural achievements.

Some scholars caution that geometric patterns could have arisen from practical needs, not purely symbolic intentions; over-interpreting ancient scratches risks building new myths about our ancestors that may be hard to verify.

The study shows how new analytical tools—like geometric morphometrics—can reopen old artifact collections and reveal hidden patterns. This is part of a broader shift in archaeology, where statistical rigour uncovers widespread capacities for abstraction across early Homo sapiens populations.

Future excavations may uncover even older examples of such engravings. Combining these finds with cognitive neuroscience could help pinpoint when and how the brain evolved to handle abstract geometry, and might challenge the traditional ‘creative explosion’ theory that focused on Europe.
